# Whether cursor's partial_tool_call can open a tool call's row before the
# call's exec arrives: whether a partial names its tool, which id the exec
# that follows repeats, and how the partials, the execs and the tool-call
# updates interleave across a turn's steps.
#
# The recording D559 is built on (bead ganja-code-gzkn;
# .omc/handoffs/2026-09-15-cursor-partial-tool-call.md, "W1 result and the
# recording"). One live turn against api2.cursor.sh, run by the user: no lane
# and no lead ran one, and nothing here was read out of auth.json. What the
# wire itself said is in the run's own debug log; the line numbers below are
# that file's. The log was grepped for the three credential markers (a bearer
# prefix, a key prefix, a JWT header) before a line of this was written: zero
# hits over :46000-:47200.
#
# Recorded by: W1's own debug lines, no scaffolding. decode.rs's
#              `a tool-call update` (one per partial_tool_call = 7,
#              tool_call_started = 2 and tool_call_completed = 3), cursor.rs's
#              `bridging an exec to a ganja tool` (carrying W1's exec_id) and
#              bridge.rs's `answering a bridged exec from the engine's result`.
#              The lines under "the lines" are verbatim copies of those three
#              families and of nothing else in the log.

#         session ran to 16:31 (2026-09-15 01:28 - 01:31 JST; the log file is

== what it settles ==
# 1. One partial per call, at the start of the call's generation, and never
#    again. The write's partial is :46255 (16:28:56.053); its next update is
#    tool_call_started at :47054, 51.26 s later, in the same instant as its
#    exec (:47055, 15 us after). The span between holds no update for the
#    write at all.
# 2. args_text_delta is empty on every partial: `args_bytes=0` on all four
#    (:46221, :46255, :47066, :47074). There is no argument text to stream
#    or to render from this arm.
# 3. The partial carries the exec's id. Each partial's `call` is the id its
#    exec is bridged under (`call=` on the bridging line, which is
#    McpArgs.tool_call_id) and the `mcp_call` its own started line reports.
#    `model_call` is `<uuid>-<step>-<4 chars>`, and it is the model step's id
#    rather than the call's: the read and the grep share `-2-x4n1`
#    (:47066, :47074). ExecRequest.exec_id is a separate uuid.
# 4. The partial does not name the tool. Every partial reports
#    `tool_call="mcp_tool_call (15)"` with no mcp_name, mcp_tool_name,
#    mcp_call or mcp_provider: the McpToolCall is present and names nothing.
#    The name first appears on tool_call_started, which arrives with the exec.
#    So at the moment a row could appear, the wire knows that an mcp call is
#    being composed and which id it will carry, not which tool it is.
# 5. Two calls in one step: the grep's partial (:47074, 16:29:52.414853)
#    arrived between the read's started (:47073, .414850) and the read's exec
#    (:47075, .414860), before the read was answered (:47077, .542571). The
#    grep's own exec came after that answer (:47092, .989525), so the read's
#    step ended while the grep was still being composed.
# 6. Every call was mcp_tool_call: no native arm appears on any update, and
#    every exec is kind="mcp_args". Native partials stay unmeasured.
# 7. One exec had no partial, no started, no completed and no exec_id:
#    exec=74, a `read` (:46284, 16:28:56.677636), 0.62 s after the write's
#    partial and 50.63 s before the write's exec. That is cursor's own
#    read-before-write, bridged as if the model had asked (bead
#    ganja-code-quc2). It paused the write's step, so the write too was
#    still being composed when a step ended. There is no partial to announce
#    it from.

== what D559 does with it ==
# The row opens on the partial and is renamed when the exec lands: the same
# id (3) under the real name, since the partial has no name to give (4).
# Only an mcp partial announces (6). What a person sees, at the recorded
# times. A rename lands when the exec's step ends, which is the exec's own
# time plus the bridge's 50 ms gather window:
#
#   bash   `● …` from 16:28:51.306, `● Bash(…)` from the exec at 16:28:52.118
#   write  `● …` from 16:28:56.053. The read cursor asked for at 16:28:56.678
#          ends that step, and the engine runs only the read; the write's row
#          stays open, withheld and not run (7). `● Write(…)` from the exec
#          at 16:29:47.309: 51.26 s of a visible row where ddf8e45 showed the
#          working line alone.
#   read   `● …` from 16:29:51.752, `● Read(…)` from the exec at 16:29:52.415
#   grep   `● …` from 16:29:52.415. The read's step ends with it still
#          composing (5); `● Grep(…)` from the exec at 16:29:52.990.
#
# Two of the four announced calls, the write and the grep, cross a step
# boundary before they are named. That is why the engine withholds a row
# still named `…` from `prepare`, keeps it open in the message while the
# step ran something, and renames it in place on whichever step names it,
# rather than renaming only within one step.

== what this recording does NOT settle ==
# - What a native partial carries (shell_tool_call, read_tool_call, ...).
#   None was seen, so a native partial announces nothing.
# - Whether cursor ever sends a second partial for a call, or a partial after
#   its exec. None was seen. The wire announces an id once and never after an
#   exec claimed it, so either would be harmless.
# - An exec whose McpArgs.tool_call_id is empty. None was seen. The wire mints
#   an id for one, which no partial could have announced, so a row a partial
#   opened for it would be closed unrun when the turn ends.
# - Why exec=74 carried no exec_id (bead ganja-code-quc2).
